samples.summary: The thirty-day sweep is scoped to the signed-in user, so a departed user's document content is never collected and persists indefinitely on a shared device
samples.evidence:
`collectStale()` builds `mine` from `headerKeysWhere(BY_USER, IDBKeyRange.only(this.userId))` (line 893-895) and then skips every aged key with `if (!mine.has(docKey)) continue;` (line 903). `dropArchivesWhere(BY_ARCHIVED_AT, range, this.userId)` (line 915-919) is scoped the same way, and `orphanSnapshotKeys()` skips other users via `belongsToAnotherUser` (line 982). The only caller is `OfflineRuntime`, which constructs the store with `userId = String(me.id)` of whoever is signed in (offline-runtime.tsx:55-62, PrivateRoute.tsx:35).

Attack/exposure chain: user A enables offline saving on a shared or borrowed machine and edits documents; A's session later ends without a deliberate "Log out" (see the 401 finding below), or A simply never returns. User B then signs in. Every sweep from then on runs with `this.userId = B`, so A's snapshots, change logs and archives — full gzip'd document content — are filtered out of the candidate set on line 903 and are never deleted. There is no origin-wide or unattributed-row cleanup: `dropAllForUser`, `purgeDocument`, `purge` and `evictOldest` are all user-scoped too. The content stays on disk until the browser profile is wiped. Every other cleanup path in this change explicitly names this sweep as its backstop (`workspaces.ts:92` "a failure leaves the thirty-day sweep to it", `offline-erase.ts:115`, `documents.ts:163`), so those paths' residual risk is unbounded rather than thirty days.

samples.summary: Access revoked by another user (workspace member removal) never purges the removed member's locally persisted copies; the comment asserting a cleanup that does not exist makes the gap read as covered
samples.evidence:
`removeMember` gates the purge on `isOfflineUser(String(userId))` (line 137), which is correct for the caller's own device — but the comment on line 130-131 claims "The removed member's own device cleans up when they next open the app." No such code exists. `OfflineRuntime` (components/offline-runtime.tsx:74-97) runs exactly two things on mount: `store.collectStale()` and `offerRecoverableWork()`. Neither consults the server for what the user may still read; there is no reconciliation of stored `docKey`s against `fetchDocuments()` or any permission endpoint.

Concretely: an owner removes collaborator B from a workspace (or from wafflebase entirely) from the owner's browser. B's device holds full, decompressible copies — snapshot plus change log — of every document in that workspace B had opened with offline saving on. Nothing on B's device deletes them. The only backstop is `collectStale`, which is thirty days at best and, per the finding above, never runs at all if B does not sign in on that device again. The same hole applies to any server-side downgrade of B's role to viewer, or removal of B from a single document, since no client-side purge is wired to those either.

The design document states the rule this violates outright: "content must not outlive the authority to read it" (docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md, § Storage cleanup table: "Document deleted, or workspace access lost | Drop that entry").

samples.summary: Session expiry (401) deliberately skips the offline erase and leaves the recorded identity in localStorage, so the commonest way a session ends on a shared machine leaves full document content on disk
samples.evidence:
The 401 arm of `fetchWithAuth` calls `logout({ ..., eraseLocalData: false })` (line 258), so `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` is not invoked (line 121-123) and `rememberOfflineUser(undefined)` — which is only reached from inside that function (offline-erase.ts:119) — never runs. Two consequences on a shared or public machine:

1. The user's snapshots, change logs and archives stay in IndexedDB. The reasoning in the comment (they will "log straight back in on the same device") holds for the author's own laptop and not for the shared-workstation case the whole feature is justified by — and a user who closes the tab and walks away never issues a deliberate `logout()` at all, so `eraseLocalData: true` is only reached by someone who clicks "Log out".
2. `wafflebase-offline-user` (offline-erase.ts:53) is left in localStorage holding the departed user's id, a persistent identifier of who last used the machine, readable by the next visitor and by any same-origin script.

Combined with the user-scoped `collectStale` finding, the retention here is not bounded by thirty days: if the next person to sign in is somebody else, the sweep filters the departed user's rows out permanently.

samples.summary: `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout` forgets the identity before the erase has succeeded and swallows the failure, so a transient IndexedDB error at logout permanently strands document content with no retry path
samples.evidence:
`const who = offlineUserId(); rememberOfflineUser(undefined); if (!who) return;` (lines 118-120) clears both the module state and the `wafflebase-offline-user` localStorage mirror *before* `eraseOfflineData(store, who)` is attempted, and the attempt's failure is caught and downgraded to `console.warn` (lines 124-130). `logout()` then shows `toast.success('Logged out successfully')` (api/auth.ts:129) and redirects.

So if `store.dropAllForUser(who)` rejects — the database is blocked by another tab's connection (`open()` rejects on `onblocked`, wafflebase-doc-store.ts:373-379), storage is momentarily unavailable, or a transaction aborts — the user is told the sign-out succeeded while their document content remains on the device, and the identity needed to retry is gone. A later `eraseOfflineDataOnLogout()` finds no `who` and returns immediately (line 120-122). Per the first finding, `collectStale` will also never reach those rows if a different account signs in next. Recording the identity only after a confirmed erase, or leaving it in place on failure, would keep the promise retryable.

samples.summary: Archives are exempt from access-loss purging and the recovery path re-materializes the whole document, letting a user create a permanent copy of content they are no longer authorized to read
samples.evidence:
`purgeDocument` deliberately spares archives (lines 753-757: "Archives are deliberately left alone"), and `purgeOfflineDocuments` — the function `deleteDocument`, `deleteDocuments`, `deleteWorkspace` and `removeMember` all call — routes only through `purgeDocument` (offline-erase.ts:154). Meanwhile `document-purged` ("the document was deleted or GC'd upstream") is one of the three `LocalChangesDropped` paths that create an archive in the first place.

The archive is not a diff of the user's unsent edits: `remove()` stores `record.snapshot` — the entire serialized document — alongside the log (lines 697-708), and `rehydrateArchive` rebuilds the full root, which `readContent` then reads whole (offline-copy-recovery.ts:202, offline-copy.ts `rehydrateArchive`). `recoverOfflineCopy` passes that to `createDocument` + `applyImportedContent` (offline-copy-recovery.ts:210-212), producing a new document owned by the recovering user.

Chain: an owner deletes a shared document (or a collaborator is removed and the document is subsequently GC'd for them) → the collaborator's SDK emits `document-purged` → `remove()` archives the full document → on the collaborator's next sign-in `OfflineRuntime` shows "Save a copy" (offline-runtime.tsx:148-156) → clicking it creates a permanent document in the collaborator's own workspace containing the entire content, including the parts they did not author, after the owner revoked it. The archive is only dropped once that copy is written (line 212), so declining the offer keeps the content and re-offers it every session.

samples.summary: `isOpenInAnyTab` matches durable lock names across accounts, so one signed-in user can observe which documents another account on the same device has open
samples.evidence:
The lock name is `wb-durable:{userId}:{docKey}` (`durableLockName`), but the match deliberately ignores the user segment: `lock.name.startsWith('wb-durable:') && lock.name.endsWith(suffix)` where `suffix = ':' + documentKeyOf(key)`. The accompanying test states this outright — "the question is about the document, so the user segment is not matched" (durable-session.test.ts, "reports a document held by any tab as open"). `navigator.locks.query()` is origin-wide, so any script on the origin running as user B can enumerate held `wb-durable:` names and learn both the numeric user id and the document key of every document user A has open in another tab of the same profile.

The practical blast radius is small — it requires two accounts concurrently signed in in one browser profile, which already implies shared physical access — and the conservative match is what makes the eviction guard safe. Hardening would be to compare the full `wb-durable:{this.userId}:{docKey}` name for the liveness decision and treat other users' locks as opaque, which loses nothing: this store never evicts another user's entry anyway (`evictOldest` intersects with `mine`, line 1126).

verdict.reason: The absence claim holds under a closed enumeration. All local deletion in the frontend flows through WafflebaseDocStore.purge/purgeDocument/dropAllForUser/dropArchive (wafflebase-doc-store.ts:733,759,827,842); grepping those names across all of packages/ yields only offline-erase.ts (logout erase, disable-watcher erase, purgeOfflineDocuments), the store's own collectStale/evictOldest, and tests. purgeOfflineDocuments has exactly four call sites — documents.ts:167, documents.ts:215, workspaces.ts:120, workspaces.ts:144 — all actor-initiated deletes. The victim-side runtime (offline-runtime.tsx:50-97, mounted at PrivateRoute.tsx:35) runs only rememberOfflineUser, watchForOfflineDisable, collectStale and offerRecoverableWork; the sole fetchDocuments() call in the frontend is workspaces.ts:96, used only by the actor-side purge. No 403/404 handler anywhere touches the store. So removeMember's comment at workspaces.ts:130-131 ("The removed member's own device cleans up when they next open the app") asserts a cleanup that does not exist: after an owner removes collaborator B, B's device retains full snapshot+change-log copies of the workspace's documents, backstopped only by the 30-day collectStale that runs solely if B signs in again. This violates the in-repo rule at docs/design/offline-local-persistence.md:242 and wafflebase-doc-store.ts:726 ("content must not outlive the authority to read it"), and is in-lane as sensitive data retained past revocation of access, with a comment that makes the gap read as covered.
